sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for Pali (pali1273, catalog kind not determinable, deciding sources Geiger 1916/1943 sec. 4 and Warder p. 4): Jacobi 1913, IF 31: 211-221. It is squarely about Pali word accent (title: '..und über die Betonung in diesen Sprachen'). Public-domain scans of the volume are open on archive.org; I downloaded the Berlin/UofT scan (whole-volume PDF and scanned), extracted the article as an 11-page PDF, cross-checked the scanned against the Digital Library of India scan and against rendered page images of pp. 218-219, and ledgered everything in (plus an addendum). Reading: Jacobi argues from ca. 75 Pali and 180 Jaina-Prakrit sandhi cases that Pali had an expiratory an earlier reading accent dependent on the quantity of the penult (heavy penult accented, Latin-like, following Bühler on modern Sanskrit pronunciation), but he leaves the exact placement conditions open (p. 221) and notes evidence for accented long finals and an initial 'Aufton' (p. 220). This is the primary source behind the Geiger sec. 4 hedge the catalog already quotes; it REFINES rather than contradicts the not determinable coding (a hedged internal reconstruction, later set aside by von Hinüber sec. 159 / Oberlies 2001 p. 17 n. 2, is the only positive claim on record). Suggested action: add Jacobi 1913 to the per-language bibliography (it was not already listed) and cite it in the record note as the source of the 'Sanskritic/Latin-type accent' hypothesis; no change to the classification. Nothing left unread; acquisition priority none. Related leads seen only as citations inside the article (not downloaded, not in the list of works with stress in the title): Jacobi 1893, ZDMG 47: 574ff. ('Die Betonung im klassischen Sanskrit und in den Prakritsprachen'); Jacobi, KZ 35: 578ff; Pischel, KZ 34: 568ff., 35: 140ff. and Grammatik der Prakrit-Sprachen sec. 46; Grierson, ZDMG 49: 395ff.org's search API and direct downloads only; the de Gruyter DOI landing page could not be reached by automated download and was not needed.

new_statements.quote: Die Reduktionen, die im Nachlaute schwerer Pänultima eintreten, sind zweifellos durch einen expiratorischen Akzent verursacht, der auf der vorletzten Silbe liegt. Und darin liegt die eigentliche Bedeutung der von mir gemachten Beobachtungen, daß nunmehr der Charakter der Betonung im Pāli und Prakrit der Jainas als Intensitätsbetonung (Iktusakzent), und ein Hauptprinzip derselben, nämlich die Abhängigkeit dieses Iktusakzentes von der Quantität der vorletzten Silbe, unzweifelhaft festgestellt sind. [...] Es muß weiterer Untersuchung überlassen bleiben, die genaueren Bedingungen ausfindig zu machen, von denen die Stelle des Iktusakzentes im Pāli und Prakrit abhing.
new_statements.translation: The reductions that occur in the wake of a heavy penult are without doubt caused by an expiratory accent lying on the penultimate syllable. And therein lies the real significance of my observations: that the character of accentuation in Pali and Jaina Prakrit as intensity accentuation (ictus accent), and one main principle of it, namely the dependence of this ictus accent on the quantity of the penultimate syllable, are now established beyond doubt. [...] It must be left to further investigation to find out the more precise conditions on which the position of the ictus accent in Pali and Prakrit depended.
new_statements.citation: Jacobi, Hermann. 1913. Über eine neue Sandhiregel im Pāli und im Prakrit der Jainas und über die Betonung in diesen Sprachen. Indogermanische Forschungen 31: 211-221.
new_statements.locator: pp. 218-219 (end of p. 218 running onto p. 219); hedge at p. 221
new_statements.reading: Jacobi reconstructs, from sandhi vowel reductions in the canonical texts, a quantity-sensitive stress (an earlier reading) accent for Pali: a heavy penult attracts the accent, in the manner of Latin. He explicitly does not state a complete placement rule (what happens after a light penult, whether long finals are accented, an initial-syllable secondary prominence), and says so at p. 221. It is an internal-reconstruction hypothesis about a dead literary language, not a description of a transmitted or observed pronunciation. It is the primary source behind the 'as Jacobi has suggested' clause in Geiger sec. 4 that the catalog already quotes, so it makes the catalog's not determinable coding better-founded and more precise: the only positive claim on record is a hedged reconstruction of a weight-sensitive (heavy-penult) an earlier reading, contested by Pischel (Grammatik der Prakrit-Sprachen sec. 46) and later dismissed as irrelevant to MIA phonology by von Hinüber sec. 159 / Oberlies 2001 p. 17 n. 2 (already held).

sources.note: A reconstructive (not descriptive) argument. From a newly observed sandhi rule (short sandhi vowel permitted after a heavy penult; ca. 180 Jaina-Prakrit and 75 Pali examples from Sutta Nipata, Thera-/Therigatha and prose), Jacobi infers that Pali and Jaina Prakrit had an expiratory / intensity (an earlier reading) accent whose placement depended on the quantity of the penult, i.e. a heavy penult carried the accent -- the Latin-type an earlier reading that Bühler reported for modern Sanskrit pronunciation ('der im allgemeinen dem des Lateinischen entspricht', p. 219). sources.quote: 'Nothing has been handed down to us about the nature of the Pali accent. It is, however, improbable that the ancient Indian accent was still in force. It is more likely that, as Jacobi has suggested for Pkt, the Sanskritic accent was the rule in Pali. This is suggested by the changes of vocalism in Pali, such as the weakening of a vowel after the accented syllable (in the Skt form) or its strengthening in the main accented syllable. Cf. secs. 19 foll.' (Norman's revision leaves sec. 4 substantively unchanged from the 1943 text we quote.)

sources.note: The accent statements concern the literary Prakrits (Maharastri, Sauraseni, Ardhamagadhi, Magadhi), not Pali; the book's Pali section is silent on accent. Compatible with the catalog's 'no determinable rule' coding for Pali, and with Jacobi 1913 only indirectly (Woolner's Sauraseni = classical-Sanskrit/Latin-type accent is the same type Jacobi reconstructs for Pali, but Woolner does not say so of Pali).
